query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The wear resistance of high-entropy alloy (HEA) protective coatings is primarily governed by a stress‐induced dynamic phase transformation that produces an ultra‐nanocrystalline or amorphous surface layer, which reduces shear strength and friction during sliding.
generation.material_initial_state: Coarse-grained, single-phase HEA protective coating (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi) produced, for instance, by additive manufacturing.
generation.intervention: Conduct controlled sliding wear tests under varying sliding speeds and contact stresses in an inert or UHV environment, while monitoring the surface microstructure in situ using TEM or synchrotron diffraction.
generation.conditions: Low-to-moderate temperature wear tests (<600 °C) in chemically inert conditions to suppress tribochemical oxidation and reactive nanocomposite formation.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a dynamically induced ultra‐nanocrystalline (or amorphous) surface layer via grain refinement (dynamic amorphization) under high contact stresses.
generation.mechanism: Under sliding wear, localized high shear stresses trigger a dynamic transformation in the near-surface region. This leads to dramatic grain refinement or amorphization, reducing the shear strength and friction at the interface, which in turn lowers wear rates compared to a material that remains coarse-grained.
generation.predicted_outcome: When the wear tests are run under conditions expected to induce dynamic amorphization, an in situ observation of an ultra‐nanocrystalline or amorphous surface layer should coincide with reductions in both friction coefficient and wear rate relative to the baseline coarse-grained state.
generation.baseline: A HEA coating in its original coarse-grained state, subjected to lower sliding speeds or contact stresses that do not induce significant dynamic microstructural evolution, which maintains a higher friction coefficient and wear rate.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold under low-to-moderate temperatures and inert environments where tribochemical effects (such as oxidation-driven glaze formation) are minimal. At higher temperatures or in oxidizing conditions, alternative mechanisms may dominate.
generation.uncertainty: While the dynamic formation of an ultra‐nanocrystalline layer is supported by earlier studies, the exact critical stress conditions and grain size thresholds for triggering this transformation may vary with alloy composition and testing parameters. Further, overlapping tribochemical processes at elevated temperatures could complicate observations.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform real-time in situ TEM or synchrotron diffraction during a series of sliding wear tests on HEA coatings, where sliding speed and contact stress are systematically increased in a UHV environment while keeping temperatures below 600 °C.
measurements: In situ imaging to quantify the formation and evolution of the surface microstructure (detection of ultra‐nanocrystalline/amorphous layer)
Friction coefficient recording throughout the test
Wear rate quantification via post-test metrology
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If advanced in situ characterization does not reveal the formation of an ultra‐nanocrystalline or amorphous surface layer under conditions that are expected to induce dynamic amorphization, or if the anticipated drop in friction coefficient and wear rate is not correlated with the microstructural change, the mechanistic hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Thus, if cooperative heterostructures capable of releasing frictional stress in stages are configured in the alloy, it is expected to suppress the sliding-induced deformation. In contrast, upon wear at high temperatures (≥600 °C), the wear behavior of the material becomes quite complex, stemming from the prevalence of surface adhesion and tribo-oxidation at the friction interface [,]. High-temperature sliding tends to soften the metallic surface that endows the near-surface material susceptible to chemical instability caused by counterbody materials or environmental oxygen, triggering severe delamination wear and composition segregation at the friction interface that exacerbates wear [,]. Materials become more dependent on tribochemical protection upon high-temperature wear due to deterioration in stiffness [,]. Tribo-oxidation may promote the formation of a protective oxide layer (glaze layer) consisting of various nanocrystalline (NC) oxides on the worn surface, which assists in enhancing the friction interface while providing solid lubrication [,,]. If the worn surface is replaced by a glaze layer as tribo-oxidation accumulates, a gentle wear scenario can be achieved. Neverthele

AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties

In the present context of sliding contacts, dynamic amorphization refers to the continuous shear-induced generation of a structurally amorphous layer that accommodates deformation. This is in competition with stress- and temperature-driven grain growth and recrystallization, all of which reestablish crystallinity and order in the shear layer. The shear layer must be amorphized again in subsequent contact passes, thus we refer to this process as dynamic amorphization.

The dark contrast regions on the order of a few nm in Fig. 2B are voids attributed to cavitation. As voids can be more thermodynamically stable than similarly sized grains, they are likely an indication of finer grain size present during sliding. Ex situ techniques like nanoindentation and electron microscopy are not an ideal way to determine the grain size of ultra-nanocrystalline surface shear layers during sliding contact for most metals, as these layers are extremely thin and naturally predisposed to rapid grain growth and recrystallization. decision.trend: Early work on HEA coatings largely focused on correlating bulk mechanical properties (e.g., hardness) and phase changes (such as those induced during plasma spraying) with wear performance. This was then refined by studies that showed how wear could trigger dynamic microstructural changes—like the formation of an ultra‐nanocrystalline surface layer (dynamic amorphization) observed via inverse Hall–Petch behavior—and even reactive transformations leading to in situ oxide nanocomposites. In other words, researchers moved from establishing phenomenological correlations to probing how wear-induced microstructural evolution (phase transitions, grain refinement, tribolayer formation) might drive wear resistance.
decision.unsolved: A clear, single mechanistic factor remains unresolved. Specifically, it is still unclear whether the dominant control of wear performance arises from lattice distortion–driven dynamic amorphization (or grain refinement), tribologically induced phase transformations, or reactive formation of protective nanocomposites. Direct, time-resolved evidence linking these in situ microstructural transitions to improvements in wear resistance is missing.
decision.lever: Perform in situ TEM or synchrotron diffraction during controlled wear tests (with systematic variation of sliding speed, contact stress, and temperature) to directly capture the initiation and evolution of phase transformations (e.g., dynamic amorphization) and nanocrystallization events in the surface layers.
decision.why: This approach follows the trend of probing microstructural evolution during wear and directly tests the hypothesis that stress‐induced dynamic phase transformation governs wear performance. By observing these changes in real time under controlled variations, the experiment will distinguish whether the emergence of a protective ultra-nanocrystalline (or transformed) surface layer is the key mechanism, thereby fulfilling the need for a single, testable, mechanistic explanation.
